extracted.intended_audience: general readers / students of Montaigne and early modern philosophical essays
extracted.subtask_description: Interpreting and extracting the normative principles and evaluative maxims Montaigne advances in these essays on fame, belief, testimony, ignorance, and knowledge. Useful for readers studying Montaigne's epistemic and moral guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fame should be reserved for rare and exemplary actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Fame is not prostituted at so cheap a rate: rare and exemplary actions, to which it is due, would not endure the company of this prodigious crowd of petty daily performances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that honour and renown ought to attach only to deeds that combine novelty and difficulty; routine useful acts (repairing a wall, cleansing a sewer) may be noticed publicly but do not merit true renown among sensible people. One should 'learn to be no more greedy, than we are capable, of glory' and disdain the mendicant thirst for honour that seeks praise by abject means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions done without ostentation are more laudable
rubrics_metrics.description: All things truly seem more laudable to me that are performed without ostentation, and without the testimony of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne values deeds that 'slip from the hand' negligently and are later discovered and raised to light by an honest person. He distrusts effects performed for 'noise' or display, and regards modest, silent benefactions as possessing greater grace and lustre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conserve and continue can be preferable to innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovation is of great lustre; but ‘tis interdicted in this age ... To forbear doing is often as generous as to do; but ‘tis less in the light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While novelty has appeal, Montaigne counsels restraint: conserving and continuing established good practices may be more prudent than seeking novelty for its own sake, especially in unsettled times where change brings inconvenience or uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on effects rather than causes when causes are irrelevant
rubrics_metrics.description: The knowledge of causes only concerns him who has the conduct of things; ... Effects concern us, but the means not at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For ordinary people, understanding how something works is less important than whether it works for their needs. Montaigne warns against the free and roving use of reason that invents causes unnecessarily; such speculation can interrupt the practical use of the world and of ourselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask 'Is it done?' before 'How is it done?'
rubrics_metrics.description: They commonly begin thus: 'How is such a thing done?' Whereas they should say, 'Is such a thing done?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne recommends grounding inquiry in the existence or facticity of the matter before expending effort on explanations. This is an epistemic rule to avoid building elaborate accounts of things that may not exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware the tendency to invent and embellish testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: We naturally make a conscience of restoring what has been lent us, without some usury and accession of our own. The particular error first makes the public error, and afterwards, in turn, the public error makes the particular one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports and rumours grow by accretion: witnesses and tellers habitually add inventions to stories to meet resistance or embellish them. Montaigne illustrates this with local miracles and childish farces that escalate; he urges caution about accepting multiplied testimony without scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate number or antiquity of believers with truth
rubrics_metrics.description: For my part, what I should not believe from one, I should not believe from a hundred and one: and I do not judge opinions by years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne insists that majority opinion and long-standing consensus are poor tests for truth. The 'multitude of fools' can protect falsehoods; plurality is not a reliable indicator of veracity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspend judgment on extraordinary claims; require extraordinary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: I am of St. Augustine’s opinion, that, 'tis better to lean towards doubt than assurance, in things hard to prove and dangerous to believe. ... He ought then only to be believed when authorised by a supernatural approbation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With miracles and supernatural claims Montaigne recommends skepticism: accept divine testimony only where properly authorized, and prefer doubt to rash affirmation. He gives examples of supposed miracles that dissolve under investigation and argues for provisional withholding of belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use modest, qualifying language and confess ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: I love these words which mollify and moderate the temerity of our propositions: 'peradventure; in some sort; some; 'tis said, I think.' ... Whoever will be cured of ignorance must confess it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne values linguistic modesty—phrases that signal probability rather than dogmatic assertion. He even proposes training children to answer inquisitively rather than assertively. Confessing ignorance is an epistemic virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: There is a 'strong and generous' kind of ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a sort of ignorance, strong and generous, that yields nothing in honour and courage to knowledge; an ignorance which to conceive requires no less knowledge than to conceive knowledge itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne distinguishes a humble, reflective ignorance (grounded in experience and discernment) from mere lack of learning. This cultivated ignorance is admirable and requires intellectual maturity to adopt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be ready to suspend judgment when evidence is insufficient (judicial modesty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let us have some form of decree that says, 'The court understands nothing of the matter' more freely and ingenuously than the Areopagites did ... ordered the parties to appear again after a hundred years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When matters cannot be unraveled, an honest admission of not knowing is preferable to forced resolution. Montaigne praises institutional modesty in judicial or public determinations as a safeguard against error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value simplicity and ordinary exemplars over learned pomp
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates ... set up not only the most regular, but the most high and vigorous beliefs, actions, and manners ... by these common and natural springs, by these ordinary and popular fancies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne admires plainness and natural wisdom (exemplified by Socrates and Cato) over ostentatious learning and elevated rhetoric. Simplicity that serves life is more valuable than learned pomp that obscures human usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temper appetite for knowledge; not all learning nourishes
rubrics_metrics.description: We carry intemperance into the study of literature, as well as into everything else. ... there are some [studies] that only burden and overcharge the stomach, instead of nourishing; and, moreover, some that, under colour of curing, poison us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne warns that excessive craving for learning can corrupt the mind: some knowledge burdens rather than benefits the soul. He notes the virtue of vows of intellectual humility—'vow ignorance'—to blunt appetite for excessive study and protect inner health.
